text: Everything so far in this chapter has been about looking at spend on demand — opening a report and reading what already happened. Budgets and anomaly alerts flip that around. A budget is a threshold you set once that watches spend continuously and notifies someone the moment it's crossed. An anomaly alert goes further — it needs no threshold at all, because it's built to catch an unusual pattern, a sudden spike that's unusual for one resource or account, even while the month's running total is nowhere near any budget.

That's the real split: a budget catches 'we're going to blow past what we planned to spend this month.' An anomaly alert catches 'something changed abruptly today,' even on day three, long before any monthly threshold would trip. A team wants both, because they're watching for two different failure shapes, not the same one at two sensitivities.

An Azure Budget lives in Cost Management and Billing, scoped the same way Cost Analysis is. Using illustrative numbers only: set an amount and a time period, say ten thousand dollars a month, scoped to one team's tagged spend. Add alert thresholds as percentages of that amount — eighty percent, a hundred percent — each wired to an action group, which can email someone, hit a webhook, or trigger a Function, so a crossed threshold does more than just notify a human.

AWS Budgets cover more ground than one number. Cost budgets are the direct equivalent of an Azure Budget. Usage budgets track a unit like EC2 instance hours instead of dollars. Coverage budgets alert when usage covered by a Savings Plan or Reservation drops below a target — a signal usage shifted or a commitment expired. Every threshold can fire off actual spend or a forecast, so a forecasted threshold can warn before the month is even over.

Anomaly detection doesn't wait for a threshold at all. Azure's runs automatically once enabled on a subscription, learning its own historical spend pattern and flagging a day that deviates from it. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection works the same way: define a monitor scoped to a service, account, or tag, and AWS applies machine-learning detection against that scope's history. When it fires, the alert names the top contributor — the specific service or resource that drove the change — usually the fastest route to root cause.

Put the four lessons together and this chapter is one pipeline: FinOps explains who's responsible, Cost Analysis and Cost Explorer are how you look at spend, tagging makes that attributable to the right team, and budgets plus anomaly detection make the system proactive — catching a spike within days instead of as a surprise on next month's invoice. Chapter 6 picks up here, turning that visibility into real optimization.
